html:
The Roman land law passed in 133 BCE by the tribune Tiberius Gracchus. It set up a three-man commission to share out state land in Italy among poor citizens.

Rome owned huge tracts of public land taken in its wars. An old rule capped how much one person could hold, but rich families had long ignored it and worked the land with slaves. The law enforced the cap, with an allowance for sons, and gave the surplus to poor citizens in small plots they could not sell. Behind it was a worry that free small farmers, the men who filled the legions, were disappearing.

The commission was Tiberius, his brother Gaius and his father-in-law Appius Claudius Pulcher. Tiberius passed the law in the popular assembly without the Senate's approval, and the fight over it ended in his murder. The commission still went on working for some years, and its boundary stones have been found in southern Italy.

The struggle split Roman politics into optimates and populares for the next century. The problem of landless soldiers came back with the Marian reforms.
sum: The Roman land law passed in 133 BCE by the tribune Tiberius Gracchus. It set up a three-man commission to share out state land in Italy among poor citizens.
